meta.headline: Does organic farming grow less food, and is it still better for the planet?
meta.seoTitle: Organic yields, land use and the environmental trade-off

dek.text: Pooled field comparisons find organic yields lower for every crop type, and per unit of food organic needs more land and adds nutrient pollution while using less energy.

assertions.text: In Ponisio's meta-analysis conventional yields were significantly higher than organic for all crop types, and the yield ratios of most crop types did not differ significantly from one another.
Per unit of food, organic systems used less energy, needed more land, had higher eutrophication potential and similar greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional systems.
qualifications: The qualification callout in question-2 gives the authors’ warning that this does not make conventional farming more sustainable, and the local-scale limit.

description.text: Pooled comparisons find organic yields lower on average for every crop type; per unit of food it uses more land, less energy, more nutrient pollution.

assertions.text: In Ponisio's meta-analysis conventional yields were significantly higher than organic for all crop types, and the yield ratios of most crop types did not differ significantly from one another.
Per unit of food, organic systems used less energy, needed more land, had higher eutrophication potential and similar greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional systems.
qualifications: The qualification callout in question-2 carries the authors’ limits on this comparison.

sections.name: hook
sections.heading: Does organic farming grow less food, and does that matter for the planet?

sentences.text: If an organic farm harvests less from each field, more land has to be farmed somewhere to put the same food on the table.
Videos and articles split on whether it does: some say organic falls short at harvest, while others say it grows as much food or more.

assertions.text: Several sources say organic farming yields less than conventional farming.
Other sources say organic farming yields as much as conventional farming or more.

sentences.text: This article settles the yield question first, then asks what a smaller harvest means for the environmental case for organic.

sections.name: question-1
sections.heading: Does organic farming really grow less food?

sentences.text: The science explainer channel AsapSCIENCE states that "organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones".

assertions.text: AsapSCIENCE says organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones.

quote.text: organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones
quote.speaker: AsapSCIENCE

sentences.text: The physician Mark Hyman argues the reverse, that "you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals".

assertions.text: Mark Hyman says you can grow as much food or more without the chemicals conventional farming uses.

quote.text: you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals
quote.speaker: Mark Hyman

sentences.text: The widest test in this evidence is a meta-analysis by Lauren Ponisio and colleagues, which put organic yields 19.2% below conventional, with a 95% credible interval of 15.5% to 22.9%.

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues' meta-analysis found organic yields 19.2% lower than conventional yields, with a 95% credible interval from 15.5% to 22.9%.
qualifications: The next sentences give the authors’ warning that the estimate may be too high and the narrower gaps on diversified farms; the unresolved callout below sets out the dissenting clinical report.

sentences.text: Conventional fields out-yielded organic ones significantly for every crop type in that analysis, and most crop types showed gaps of similar size.

assertions.text: In Ponisio's meta-analysis conventional yields were significantly higher than organic for all crop types, and the yield ratios of most crop types did not differ significantly from one another.

sentences.text: The authors report that their gap is smaller than the ones recent meta-analyses had found, and they caution that the literature leans towards reporting bigger conventional advantages, so even their figure may be too high.

assertions.text: Ponisio's meta-analysis found a smaller organic yield gap than recent earlier meta-analyses had reported.
Ponisio and colleagues say their yield-gap estimate may still be an overestimate.

sentences.text: Cereals, the crop type with the widest organic shortfall, made up 53% of the comparisons, so the pooled average leans towards them.

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues report that cereal crops, which showed the greatest yield difference between organic and conventional systems, were greatly over-represented at 53% of comparisons.

sentences.text: As for why organic yields lag, a review of organic food and health, citing earlier research rather than analysing yields itself, says nitrogen typically limits crop yield in organic systems but not in conventional ones.

assertions.text: Mie and colleagues' review, citing earlier work, says crop yield is typically limited by plant nitrogen availability in organic but not in conventional systems.
qualifications: The sentence says the review cites earlier work rather than analysing yields itself.

sentences.text: A separate meta-analysis of farm profitability by Crowder and Reganold lands nearby: with organic price premiums removed, gross returns, which the authors say mirror yields, were 10% lower for organic crops and 18% lower for organic systems.

assertions.text: Crowder and Reganold report that, because gross returns without premiums mirror yields, their observed yields were 10% lower for organic crops and 18% lower for organic systems, similar to the results of the yield meta-analyses.
qualifications: The sentence says these yields are read from gross returns, which the authors say mirror yields, not measured directly.

sentences.text: The dissent here is a clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics, whose abstract says well-designed farming studies demonstrate yields comparable to those of conventional farming.

assertions.text: The AAP clinical report says well-designed farming studies demonstrate organic yields comparable to those of conventional farming techniques.

sentences.text: That abstract makes its case in a single sentence, without a yield figure and without naming the studies it rests on.

assertions.text: The AAP report's abstract states comparable yields in one sentence without giving a yield figure or naming the studies.

sentences.text: So the evidence here cannot say what explains the split: the studies that measured yields or returns all found organic behind, and the abstract that disagrees does not show which comparisons it read differently.

assertions.text: On Ponisio's pooled comparisons organic yields were lower than conventional, by 19.2% on average.
qualifications: The callout states that the split is unexplained; s08 gives the overstatement warning.

assertions.text: Crowder and Reganold report that, because gross returns without premiums mirror yields, their observed yields were 10% lower for organic crops and 18% lower for organic systems, similar to the results of the yield meta-analyses.
qualifications: s12 says these yields are read from gross returns.

assertions.text: The AAP report's abstract states comparable yields in one sentence without giving a yield figure or naming the studies.

sentences.text: On the measured comparisons, then, organic farming does grow less food per field, by the 19.2% average given above, perhaps by somewhat less given the authors’ caveat.

assertions.text: On Ponisio's pooled comparisons organic yields were lower than conventional, by 19.2% on average.
qualifications: s08 carries the authors’ overstatement warning and the unresolved callout the dissenting report.

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues say their yield-gap estimate may still be an overestimate.

sentences.text: A smaller harvest from each field leads straight to the next question, about land and the environment.

sections.name: question-2
sections.heading: Is organic farming actually better for the planet?

sentences.text: Harvard Health tells its readers that "Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet".

assertions.text: Harvard Health says organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet.

quote.text: Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet
quote.speaker: Harvard Health

sentences.text: The pediatric report quoted above agrees, stating that organic farming "has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches".

assertions.text: The AAP clinical report says organic farming has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches.

quote.text: has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches

qualifications: The rest of this section gives the per-unit-of-food comparison and the qualification callout that narrow it.

sentences.text: Clark and Tilman tested this kind of claim per unit of food rather than per field, in a meta-analysis that only compared both systems within the same publication.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman compared organic and conventional systems per unit of food, limiting comparisons to within the same publication.

blocks.caption: Organic against conventional farming per unit of food, Clark and Tilman meta-analysis

cells.label: Lower greenhouse gas emissions, not significant

sentences.text: Land showed the widest range: organic systems needed 25% to 110% more of it to produce the same food.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems required 25% to 110% more land than conventional systems.
qualifications: The unresolved callout below says how wide the range is and that the yield gaps behind it may be overstated; the qualification callout gives the local-scale limit.

sentences.text: Organic used 15% less energy, but its eutrophication potential, a measure of nutrient pollution, was 37% higher.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems used 15% less energy and had 37% higher eutrophication potential than conventional systems.

sentences.text: Greenhouse gas emissions per unit of food did not differ significantly, which the authors put down to manure: relying on it turns more of the farm’s reactive nitrogen into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic and conventional systems did not significantly differ in greenhouse gas emissions.
qualifications: The qualification callout below says the comparisons are local in scale and may differ regionally, nationally or globally.

assertions.text: Reliance on manure increases the share of reactive nitrogen in organic systems that turns into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, causing similar emissions.

sentences.text: Counted per unit of food, organic is not clearly the greener system: it saves energy but takes more land and causes more nutrient pollution, with emissions about level.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems used less energy, needed more land, had higher eutrophication potential and similar greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional systems.
qualifications: The qualification callout that follows gives the authors’ warning against reading this as a win for conventional farming, and the local-scale limit.

sentences.text: The authors reject the opposite conclusion too: conventional farming needs more energy and leans on heavy fertiliser, herbicide and pesticide inputs that can harm health and the environment, so their results do not make it the more sustainable system.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman say organic systems' higher land use and eutrophication should not be taken to mean conventional systems are more sustainable, since conventional practices need more energy and rely on high nutrient, herbicide and pesticide inputs that can harm human health and the environment.

sentences.text: Because each comparison sits inside one publication, the results describe differences at a local scale, and the authors say the balance could change at a regional, national or global scale.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman say their within-publication results indicate differences at a local scale and that impacts might differ at a regional, national or global scale.

sentences.text: The extra land is a wide range rather than a single figure, and it rests on yield gaps that Ponisio and colleagues think the published literature may overstate.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems required 25% to 110% more land than conventional systems.
qualifications: The sentence states the range is wide.

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues say their yield-gap estimate may still be an overestimate.

sentences.text: The emissions result is an absence of a significant difference, not a measured tie: organic came out 4% lower, a gap the analysis could not separate from chance, and the comparisons are local in scale.

assertions.text: Organic and conventional systems did not significantly differ in greenhouse gas emissions per unit of food, although these were 4% lower in organic systems.
Clark and Tilman say their within-publication results indicate differences at a local scale and that impacts might differ at a regional, national or global scale.

sentences.text: What matters far more is the food itself: on every indicator they examined, ruminant meats had 20 to 100 times the impacts of plant-based foods, a gap much larger than the one between farming systems.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman found ruminant meats have impacts 20 to 100 times those of plant-based foods for all indicators examined, and that the difference between foods is large compared to the difference between production systems.
qualifications: The qualification callout above gives the local-scale limit of the farming-system comparisons.

sentences.text: That contrast sets foods against each other; the farming-system differences it dwarfs come from local comparisons, which the authors say could look different at a regional, national or global scale.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman found ruminant meats have impacts 20 to 100 times those of plant-based foods for all indicators examined, and that the difference between foods is large compared to the difference between production systems.
Clark and Tilman say their within-publication results indicate differences at a local scale and that impacts might differ at a regional, national or global scale.

sections.name: close
sections.heading: What to ask when organic is sold as more food or a greener choice

sentences.text: When someone says organic grows as much as conventional, ask what was measured and how many comparisons stand behind the claim.
When a product is sold as better for the planet, ask whether that holds per field or per unit of food, and which food is on the plate.
